# Talk about making love before you do it

I use “making love” differently from just having sex. Making love, to me, is when two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected use sex as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced that kind of love, explaining it may be like explaining the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know; I’d suggest starting with my inner-child reparenting guide instead.

Having sex is the physical act itself, whether that connection is there or not, and sometimes the act creates more of the connection too.

The awkward part is that most couples wait until they’re already having sex to talk honestly about it. That is about the worst time to discover that saying what you want disappoints the naked person in front of you.

Before then, I want to know what actually makes her body relax and open, what simply doesn’t work for her, and whether there’s anything kinky she needs to be able to say out loud. I want her to know the same things about me. Our pasts may have made either of us want certain things or avoid them, and neither of us has to know all the answers yet. “I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you” is a perfectly good answer.

I also want to know what sex is for her. Maybe she mainly thinks of bonding and I mainly think of play, or vice versa. Sometimes it may feel sacred; another time it may just be how we come down from a bad day. It doesn’t have to mean the same thing every time.

And sex drive won’t stay put. For some stretch one of us is going to want more, less, or something different. That mismatch can turn into a really sad quiet resentment. We can’t solve a future mismatch in advance, but I’d rather know how we plan to talk about it before either person is already hurt.

The question I care about most is whether we can still say what’s true once we’re naked. If I think she’ll be disappointed, can I tell her anyway? Can she do the same with me? Talking before our clothes come off is already part of making love to me, because bodies fitting well doesn’t tell me whether we can stay honest while we’re completely exposed.

## Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Oxytocin, vasopressin, and the rest can start attaching you anyway. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.

“I don’t know whether I want something serious with you. I’m not pretending I do. I’d still like to have sex.”

That may be candid about what you expect now. It doesn’t settle what either of you will owe if the act creates something neither of you expected. Sex can make a child. If this girl gets pregnant, she’s gonna call you. Then what? You block her? Agree to child support? Try to convince her to abort when she thinks abortion is killing her child? This is what penetrative sex can do. No contraception is perfect.

## Beware idealization in either direction

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine.

You can see something in a person before she fully lives it, but then you have to ask her:

“I see this in you, and I think it’s special. Do you wanna reach for it together?”

If she says no, forget it. You’re in la la land. If she says yes, ask what is blocking her. Is the block more than you can handle? Or does she mostly need somebody to join her on the journey and believe in her?

Partners should help each other grow. Who else is going to do it? Your mom and dad? You’re already grown. Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you’d better choose someone who helps you grow well.

results.text:
## Desire is expressed differently for men & women

Women often show wanting directly. They’ll ask for what they want, reach for the man, or even ask him to do something they could have done themselves.

Men tend to make their wanting useful: providing, fixing things, doing heavy work, trying to become indispensable. Not because men are less needy, but their neediness partly consists of being needed. Emotionally, women express their needs more, but this also allows them to get supported more often and by a wider social net. Men, on the other hand, tend to keep their needs to themselves or put them all onto their woman, especially when it comes to the need for a confidant.

If a man is too “needy,” it tends to turn women off. The way women see it, a man should be in control of himself and able to satisfy his own basic needs. After all, how is he supposed to provide for somebody else if he can't manage himself?

It's not that male pursuit is a turn-off to women (assuming they are interested in the man), but they want to see that the man can pursue strongly while staying grounded. The polarity evaporates when he keeps reaching without satisfaction, loses control of himself, or makes the woman responsible for regulating his emotions.

## Not A Performance

I don’t want masculinity or femininity turning into an identity I have to perform.

I don’t actually think of myself as especially masculine. I step into that energy when I see that a woman would appreciate it, and then it comes naturally.

If I have to prove that I’m the man, every time I hesitate, cry, need help, or get something wrong becomes a threat to the role. That feels fake to me.

Bee once called me her “wife.” I don’t recommend that as a polarity exercise, by the way.

I don’t want a woman performing femininity for me either. She shouldn’t have to act soft, helpless, or cute every minute just to prove she is feminine. Surrender means so much more when she could take control but prefers not to at that moment.

We can invite these energies out of each other gently.

results.text:
# What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” can mean almost anything. I might hear romance, sex, exclusivity, living together, shared money, children, caregiving, spiritual partnership, and family identity all bundled together, while she may mean, “We really like each other and we’ll see.” Or the reverse. I don’t mind some things staying undefined while they’re growing, but a relationship label can make two people think they agreed to a whole bundle they never actually discussed.

One honest version is basically a practical partnership. This is very common, especially outside the modern West. Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex without pretending that overwhelming romantic love is holding the whole thing together.

That feels wrong to me, probably because I’ve been in love, but I don’t think there’s anything inherently wrong with it if both people know what they’re doing. This kind of arrangement has been promoted throughout history because it isn’t based on highly fluctuating feelings. Ironically, that can also be where its instability comes from. One day one of them meets a heartthrob at work or church or somewhere else and starts wondering why they settled for less.

What I actually want is romance with enough humility to admit that I can’t guarantee a future feeling. Two people can really be in love and take the bond seriously. They can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life together, but they still can’t know exactly what their hearts will feel ten years from now.

If the romance changes, then what? Do we try to revive it? Renegotiate what we’re doing? Which parts of the life we built are supposed to remain even if the feeling changes?

My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community. Obviously most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, “Start Where You Are.” Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive.

Before I commit to one type of relationship, I want to know what we’re actually joining and why. Is this mainly a romance, a practical partnership, or both? What are we promising to do, and what are we only hoping we’ll keep feeling? If the romance changes, what is still supposed to remain?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation? Which needs should still be supported mostly outside the relationship? How do we plan on revisiting the agreement when our lives change? If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?

Those are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling. Be creative and see what you come up with. You can make a card game out of it and have some fun with it. If there’s real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.
